clue.text: Everyone's entertained by rotten song

indicators.note: a host entertains guests inside, so one word is held within the other

parts.note: rotten food has gone bad
everyone is all; the 's stands for 'is', joining the surface

explanation.surface: Every listener is having to sit through a dreadful song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Everyone's' reads as a possessive, but the 's is just 'is' smoothing the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A ballad is a narrative song or slow sentimental number, so it is a kind of song.

clue.text: Touch some cocoa butter

indicators.note: some means only a portion of the following words is taken

parts.note: the letters straddle the end of cocoa and the start of butter

explanation.surface: Dab on a little of the skin cream.
explanation.definitionFit: Things that abut share a border and are in contact with one another.

clue.text: Biography presenting false statements about fine politician

indicators.note: about means going around, so the word before wraps round the next

parts.note: lies are untrue statements
F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine
a Tory is a British Conservative politician

explanation.surface: A memoir full of fabrications about a decent Conservative MP.
explanation.walkthrough: Tory is the everyday name for a member of Britain's Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: A biography is the account of someone's life, so a life story.

clue.text: Animal put on island in Florida?

parts.note: to don clothes is to put them on
the Florida Keys are a chain of low islands; the question mark flags the example

explanation.surface: A creature placed on a Florida island.
explanation.definitionFit: A donkey is a domesticated member of the horse family, a beast of burden.

clue.text: More than one lawman spoils an artist

parts.note: to spoil something is to mar it; mars is the verb form
Frans Hals was a Dutch Golden Age portrait painter

explanation.surface: A sheriff's posse ruins a painter's day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'More than one lawman' is a roundabout way of asking for a plural noun.
explanation.definitionFit: US marshals are federal law officers, so the plural is several lawmen.

clue.text: I can't say I'm a peerless lady going astray

indicators.note: going astray means wandering off course, so these letters stray from their order

parts.note: taken as written, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: An incomparable woman is losing her way and confessing she has no words.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiomatic refusal to disclose a secret, so the speaker declines to tell.

clue.text: Nut found by bird at the end of the line

parts.note: the rail is a family of marsh birds, such as the water rail
nut is slang for head

explanation.surface: A nut is discovered by a bird perched at the end of the washing line.
explanation.walkthrough: Clue order is nut then bird, but 'found by' only means placed next to, and the bird comes first in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A railhead is the terminus of a railway, the point where the track stops.

clue.text: Intoxicated female heard scavenger

indicators.note: heard means the words are judged by their sound when spoken

parts.note: intoxicated is high, and Ena is a woman's name

explanation.surface: A drunk woman overheard a carrion-eater.
explanation.walkthrough: Female here is a girl's name, Ena, rather than a generic word like HEN or SHE.
explanation.definitionFit: Hyenas are African carnivores famous for feeding on carcasses left by other predators.

clue.text: Number called for supporters joining team

parts.note: legs hold up a body or a table
a football or cricket side has eleven players; joining places it after the first piece

explanation.surface: A rallying call for fans who are signing up with the club.
explanation.walkthrough: In British bingo the caller announces 11 as 'legs eleven', the two upright digits looking like legs.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the traditional bingo caller's phrase for the number 11.

clue.text: Champ's first painful thrashing in important match

indicators.note: a thrashing beats something about, so the letters are knocked into a new order
first asks for only the opening letter of the word before it

parts.note: the opening letter of champ
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A champion suffers a painful defeat in a big game.
explanation.definitionFit: A cup final is the deciding game of a knockout competition, so it is a high-stakes fixture.

clue.text: Look at wise man we might hear in lengthy cold spell

indicators.note: we might hear tells us the words are judged by how they sound when spoken

parts.note: to look at is to eye, and a wise man is a sage

explanation.surface: Seeing a guru apparently takes a long chilly stretch.
explanation.walkthrough: Said quickly, EYE SAGE runs together as ICE AGE.
explanation.definitionFit: An ice age is a glacial period lasting many thousands of years, the longest cold spell imaginable.

clue.text: Shake spear here — he's a farm worker

indicators.note: shaking things jumbles them, so the following letters are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written, every letter used

explanation.surface: It plays on Shakespeare: 'Shake spear here' sounds like a Bard pun pointing at a farmhand.
explanation.walkthrough: Shake looks like part of Shakespeare's name, but it is the anagram signal for the twelve letters that follow.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheep shearer clips fleeces from flocks, which is agricultural labour.

clue.text: Rich oil producer wasn't perfectly upright

parts.note: an oil well extracts crude oil
a ship that heeled leaned to one side

explanation.surface: A wealthy oil tycoon who couldn't stand up straight.
explanation.definitionFit: Well-heeled is an idiom for wealthy, from being able to afford good shoes.

clue.text: Captain in submarine movies

indicators.note: in says the letters are found inside the run of words that follows

parts.note: the letters straddle the end of submarine and the start of movies

explanation.surface: A skipper appearing in films about U-boats.
explanation.walkthrough: Captain Nemo commands the submarine Nautilus in Jules Verne's novel and its film versions, so the hiding place suits him.
explanation.definitionFit: Nemo is the fictional captain of the Nautilus in Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea.

clue.text: Jack leaves Lady Jane's bust to be carefully examined

indicators.note: something bust is broken, so the letters are smashed and reassembled
when something leaves it is taken away from the group

parts.note: J is the card abbreviation for jack; this letter is the one removed
taken as written

explanation.surface: Jack walks out on Lady Jane, and her statue is scrutinised.
explanation.walkthrough: Bust looks like a sculpture of Lady Jane, but it means broken: drop J, then rearrange the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: To analyse something is to study it closely in detail, matching the past participle here.

clue.text: Beatles hit not so long ago

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Paul McCartney's 1965 ballad recorded by the Beatles
second meaning: in the recent past

explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is the looser adverb use, as in 'it seems like only yesterday'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names the famous Beatles song and also means recently, the day before or loosely the recent past.

clue.text: Leader of band helps string players

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letter of band
to help is to assist

explanation.surface: A bandleader lends a hand to the violinists.
explanation.walkthrough: Leader of band looks like a conductor, but it only asks for one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Bassists play the double bass or bass guitar, both stringed instruments.

clue.text: Kid's companion put down floor covering in gym

indicators.note: in places the preceding words inside the abbreviation that follows

parts.note: PE, physical education, is school gym class
to put down is to lay
a mat covers part of a floor

explanation.surface: A child's friend helps set out the mats in the gym.
explanation.definitionFit: A playmate is a child's friend to play with, so a youngster's companion.

clue.text: Witnesses going back and forth

indicators.note: a word that reads the same whichever way it goes fits back and forth

parts.note: the defining word itself; the remainder of the clue says the answer reads identically either way

explanation.surface: People who saw the crime keep pacing up and down.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition and the indicator are all there is: find a four-letter verb meaning witnesses that reads the same both ways.
explanation.definitionFit: To see something happen is to witness it, so sees is the matching third-person verb.

clue.text: Changing one's residence may be poignant

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one claim that leaving home is sad; it is two separate senses.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is the present participle of relocate house, and an adjective for emotionally touching.

clue.text: Male driver sees to rotten turn?

indicators.note: a turn moves things round, so these letters are spun into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, every letter used

explanation.surface: A man at the wheel attends to a bad manoeuvre.
explanation.walkthrough: Driver suggests a motorist; here it means the thing that drives male characteristics.
explanation.definitionFit: Testosterone is the main male sex hormone, driving masculine traits and behaviour.

clue.text: Child with a large sum

parts.note: a tot is a small child
with joins; a is taken as written
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: A kid comes with a hefty amount of money.
explanation.definitionFit: A total is the whole amount when figures are added up.

clue.text: Small pale bird

parts.note: S is the clothing-size abbreviation for small
wan means pale and sickly-looking

explanation.surface: A little bird with washed-out plumage.
explanation.definitionFit: The swan is a large long-necked waterbird.

clue.text: Sort of pastel tableware

indicators.note: to sort something is to arrange it, so the letters are put in another order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Crockery in a soft pale colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Plates are flat dishes for serving and eating food, a core item of tableware.

clue.text: Put on the ground, perhaps, as specified

definitions.meaning: first meaning: placed down, as a carpet or bricks might be
second meaning: stipulated, as rules set out in writing

explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' signals that putting on the ground is only one example of the literal sense.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means physically placed down, and also prescribed, as in conditions established by law.

clue.text: Adored by fans, one did lose out

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: out suggests the letters are thrown out of place and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A star still loved by supporters even after a defeat.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone idolised is worshipped as a hero, especially by a following of admirers.

clue.text: Man approaching an area that's in South America

parts.note: a guy is a man
taken as written
A is the standard abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: A fellow walks towards a region of the South American continent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Approaching' just places the man before the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Guyana is a country on the northern coast of South America, so it is a place lying there.
